episodes.177844: A strong thunderstorm produced tree damage, which led to powerline damage, in Longwood.
episodes.178270: An ice jam developed on the Aroostook River...between Caribou and Fort Fairfield...during the afternoon of the 14th. The ice jam produced flooding which initially led to the closure of the Grimes/North Caribou Road. The flooding eventually expanded to impact the town of Fort Fairfield during the evening of the 15th where a portion of both Russell Road and Riverside Avenue were closed. The ice jam released during the late afternoon and evening of the 16th allowing river levels to fall. Roads were re-opened with the falling river levels.
episodes.178784: A weakening frontal boundary approached and stalled on the Florida Gulf coast in the morning of April 14. The increasing instability, with warm temperatures, in the afternoon led to scattered showers and thunderstorms across southeastern Florida in the late afternoon and early evening.
episodes.178852: A deeper than average snow pack from northern Minnesota into northern Wisconsin underwent a rapid melt through much of April from unseasonably warm temperatures combined with multiple rain events. This resulted in increased water levels and significant flooding for the entire length of the local Mississippi River, with most sites climbing to their third to fifth highest crests on record. Initial flood warnings were issued in mid April with peak stages realized in late April. The highest above flood stage was Winona Dam at 5.81 ft over flood stage.
episodes.178866: Scattered thunderstorms produced isolated reports of severe hail across East Tennessee.
episodes.178894: A cold front moved across eastern Nebraska which had observed unseasonably warm temperatures in the past couple of days. The front set off a line of storms that produced strong wind gusts and large hail. The strongest measured wind gust was 67 mph in Sarpy County and there were several 1.75-inch hail reports in Otoe County. A flash flood was reported in Sarpy County as 2-3 inches of rain fell across the county.
episodes.179012: Much of the Elm River drainage basin experienced a cold slow start to spring, leaving the ground frozen when temperatures finally started to consistently warm above freezing during the second week in April. Snow water equivalent at the start of April was in excess of 4 inches, with most of the melt entering waterways and the resultant flooding mainly affecting agricultural lands.||A Presidential Disaster Declaration was approved for Brown, Clark, Codington, Day, Faulk, Grant, Hand, Marshall, Potter and Roberts Counties, as well as for the Lake Traverse Indian Reservation, where an estimated $2,305,362 in total qualifying costs were incurred during spring flooding.
episodes.179140: Between 5:30-8:30 p.m. CDT on this Friday late afternoon-evening, a smattering of strong to marginally-severe thunderstorms streamed southwest-to-northeast through far southeast portions of South Central Nebraska, primarily affecting Thayer, Nuckolls, Fillmore and Clay counties. These storms yielded a handful of reports of small hail (including up to dime size in the Nelson, Lawrence and Davenport areas), but just one report of severe-criteria hail (half dollar size) in Deshler shortly after 6 p.m. CDT. ||This fairly high-based convection initiated along a well-defined cold front pushing slowly southward through the region, with this front situated from southwestern Kansas to far east-central Nebraska by late afternoon. The first cells erupted just south of the state line in north central Kansas around 5 p.m. CDT, with this activity quickly spreading northward into Nuckolls/Thayer counties between 5:30-6:30 p.m. CDT. Over the next few hours, scattered storms continued to roam southeastern portions of the local area, but by 8:30 p.m. CDT all strong to severe convection had departed eastward into southeast Nebraska. In the big picture of the mid-upper levels, the Central Plains resided just downstream from a large-scale trough approaching from the Northern/Central Rockies. As storms developed into South Central Nebraska, the mesoscale environment featured only 500-1000 J/kg mixed-layer CAPE, but strong effective deep-layer wind shear of 40-50 knots. At the surface, moisture was seasonably-scant, with dewpoints only topping out around 50 (F). Temperature-wise, the aforementioned cold front traversing the region promoted a healthy gradient across South Central Nebraska, with 6 p.m. readings ranging from only 53 degrees in Ord, to 81 in Hebron.
episodes.179141: Between 5-9 p.m. CDT on this Friday late afternoon-evening, a smattering of strong to marginally-severe thunderstorms streamed southwest-to-northeast through Jewell and Mitchell counties in the eastern part of this North Central Kansas area. These storms yielded a handful of reports of small hail (including up to dime size around Mankato), but just one report of severe-criteria hail (quarter size) east of Webber shortly after 6:30 p.m. CDT. ||This fairly high-based convection initiated along a well-defined cold front pushing slowly southward through the region, with this front situated from southwestern Kansas to far east-central Nebraska by late afternoon. The first cell of the day erupted over the heart of Jewell County around 5 p.m. CDT, dropping small hail in Mankato before departing northward into Nebraska. Around 6:30 p.m. CDT, more storms developed over northeastern Jewell County, producing the quarter size hail near Webber before also heading up into Nebraska. To the south in Mitchell County, there were no ground-truth storm reports, but a few storms sported radar indications of small hail/and or gusty winds, including one that brushed the far southeast edges of the county mainly between 7:30-8:30 p.m. CDT...shortly before all strong convection departed east of the local area for the night. In the big picture of the mid-upper levels, the Central Plains resided just downstream from a large-scale trough approaching from the Northern/Central Rockies. As storms developed over North Central Kansas, the mesoscale environment featured only 500-1000 J/kg mixed-layer CAPE, but strong effective deep-layer wind shear of 40-50 knots. At the surface, moisture was seasonably-scant, with dewpoints only topping out around 50 (F). Temperature-wise, the aforementioned cold front traversing the region promoted a healthy gradient across northern Kansas, with 6 p.m. readings ranging from only 53 degrees in Goodland, to 83 degrees in Concordia.
episodes.179316: The Mustinka River and its tributaries experienced flooding due to the rapid snowmelt in western Minnesota caused by frozen soils and a quick thaw in the second week of April. The area, including Wheaton, saw a significant snow depth of 32 inches on April 6th. As a result, a large amount of snowmelt flowed into the waterways, leading to numerous county and township roads being submerged. To safeguard properties, many communities initiated sandbagging operations.
episodes.179667: During early April, an unprecedented snow depth of 15 to 20 inches was recorded. However, a few weeks later, warmer temperatures triggered a rapid snowmelt that occurred over a span of four to five days in mid-April. This quick thaw led to extensive overland flooding in Traverse and Big Stone Counties, resulting in severe impacts to public and personal infrastructure. To protect their properties, residents took proactive measures by initiating sandbagging operations. Unfortunately, the floodwaters caused the sewer system in the city of Dumont to be overwhelmed, resulting in water backing up into streets and basements. Additionally, numerous county and township roads, as well as widespread agricultural lands, were inundated due to the snowmelt. The floodwaters gradually receded during the evening hours of April 17th.
episodes.179724: A warm front lifted through the area during the afternoon hours. Scattered showers and thunderstorms developed along the front, triggering several clusters of severe thunderstorms.
episodes.179765: A cold front initiated highly elevated showers and embedded thunderstorms during the late afternoon hours of April 14th. As this activity transitioned east, it produced strong gusty winds as high as 70 MPH. In addition to gusty winds, dry lightning was also reported along with some blowing dust.
episodes.179785: Two areas of severe weather occurred on the 14th.  One section was in north central Kansas while the other was located over south central Kansas.  The primary hazard for these events was hail one inch in diameter.
episodes.179839: A few storms moved through far western Kansas in the early evening across far western Kansas.
episodes.180055: Snowmelt flooding along the Minnesota Tributaries began in mid-April, with a few locations persisting into early May.
